analysis.one_liner: Cuts consumer liability for debit card fraud and speeds up bank error investigation.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by the chairman of the Senate Banking Committee with bipartisan support, never got a committee vote and died at the end of 1998.
analysis.plain_summary: Debit cards at the time did not carry the fraud protections that credit cards did: if a thief used your card, your bank could hold you responsible for far more than $50 and take up to ten business days to investigate. This bill would have capped what you could be charged for a fraudulent debit transaction, cut the investigation deadline to five business days, required banks to warn customers when a card could be used without a PIN, and barred banks from mailing out cards that work with just a signature. The bill went to the Senate Banking Committee and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Debit card users, who at the time could be held liable for large fraudulent withdrawals. The bill would have capped their liability at $50 for unauthorized transfers, halved the time a bank could take to investigate a disputed error, required warnings when cards lacked PIN protection, and required banks to disclose whether they would reimburse fees (like bounced-check fees) caused by a fraudulent withdrawal.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Debit card users and bank customers

how_it_helps.text: Caps consumer liability for an unauthorized debit card transfer at the lesser of $50 or the amount taken before the bank was notified, including overdraft or other fees the bank imposed as a result of the fraud [S3].
Cuts from ten business days to five the deadline for a bank to report the results of its investigation and to temporarily recredit a consumer's account after a claimed error [S2][S3].
Requires a printed warning whenever a card is issued that can be used without a PIN — meaning a stolen card could be used with just a signature [S2][S3].
Bars banks from sending out non-PIN-protected cards unless the customer requested one, applied for one, or was renewing or replacing an existing card [S2][S3].
Requires an annual summary of error-resolution procedures and disclosure of the bank's policy on reimbursing fees caused by fraud, such as returned-check fees and late charges [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other card-issuing financial institutions, which would bear the cost of faster investigations, absorbing more fraud losses under the $50 liability cap, printing disclosures, and reimbursing customer fees caused by fraudulent transfers.

drawbacks.text: Banks would absorb more fraud losses under the $50 liability cap and the shortened five-day recrediting deadline; a good-faith objection is that issuers would recoup those costs through higher account fees or by restricting debit card availability, and that tighter rules could slow the rollout of convenient signature-based debit cards [S3].

A flat $50 cap removes the existing law's graduated liability (where consumers who wait to report a loss can be liable for more), which opponents could argue reduces customer incentive to report lost cards promptly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the benefits are concrete and direct: a firm cap on what fraud can cost them and a faster path to getting money back in their account. The costs fall on banks as fraud losses and compliance work, and some of that could be passed back through fees. That tradeoff — a modest, debatable cost to issuers versus a real reduction in risk for millions of account holders — is exactly what a committee hearing would have tested. The bill never got one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read once and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Alfonse D'Amato, a Republican who chaired the Senate Banking Committee, introduced the bill on September 23, 1997, with two Republican and two Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].

The bill's entire action history is introduction and referral: it was read twice and sent to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote ever recorded [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the bill expired in committee and had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other card issuers stayed under the existing, weaker rules, keeping longer investigation windows and broader liability for customers whose cards were stolen. Debit card users got no new protections until Congress addressed the issue in later legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split across parties — two Republicans (D'Amato, Bennett) and two Democrats (Dodd, Bryan) — and no opposition was ever recorded because the bill never reached a vote [S4].

industries.industry: Banks and other debit card issuers
industries.note: The bill would shift fraud losses to issuers, cut their investigation window from ten days to five, and require new disclosures and fee reimbursements. Issuers could pass some costs back to customers, but the direct financial burden falls on them.

Rules restricting signature-only cards and unsolicited card issuance would press issuers toward PIN-protected cards, changing how networks' most convenient card format operated. Consumers would get more fraud protection as a result.
